games.objective: Partnerships bid for the right to name trumps and whether high or low cards win, then make their contract. First to 7 points wins.
quickStart: Goal: first partnership to 7 points.
Bid books over six plus uptown (high wins), downtown (low wins) or no trump.
Winner takes the kitty and names trumps. Make it to score; fail to lose the bid.
setup: Four players in two partnerships, partners opposite.
Deal 12 cards to each player and six face down to the kitty.
gameplay: Bidding: starting left of the dealer, each player bids once (or passes). A bid is a number from 3 to 7 — the ‘books’ (tricks) over six that their side will take — plus ‘uptown’ (high cards win), ‘downtown’ (low cards win) or ‘no trump’. Each bid must be higher than the last; at the same number, no trump outranks a suit bid.
The winner takes the kitty, discards six cards (which count as their side’s first book), and names trumps (unless no trump).
Uptown: cards rank A, K, Q … 2. Downtown: A, 2, 3 … K (the Ace stays highest in most rules). The Big Joker and Little Joker are the two highest trumps; in no trump they are worthless.
The bidder leads. Follow suit if you can; otherwise play any card. The highest trump wins, otherwise the best card of the suit led.
scoring: If the bidding side takes at least six books plus their bid, they score one point for each book over six. If they fail, they lose the amount of their bid.
No-trump bids often score double.
First to 7 points wins (some play to 11, or win by reaching +7 or forcing the opponents to −7).
variations: Without jokers: deal 13 each and the kitty is 4 cards, or play with no kitty.

games.name: Briscola
equipment: A 40-card Italian deck, or a standard deck with the 8s, 9s and 10s removed
games.objective: Win more than half the card points (61 of 120) in tricks.
quickStart: Goal: win 61 of the 120 card points.
Three cards in hand; no need to follow suit. Draw after each trick.
Aces (11) and 3s (10) are the big prizes; trumps beat everything.
setup: Cards rank A (high), 3, K, Q (Horse), J, 7, 6, 5, 4, 2.
Card points: Ace 11, 3 10, King 4, Queen 3, Jack 2; others 0.
Deal three cards to each player. Turn the next card face up for trumps (the ‘briscola’) and place it under the stock.
gameplay: The player right of the dealer leads (play goes counter-clockwise in Italy).
You do not have to follow suit — play any card.
The highest trump wins; otherwise the highest card of the suit led.
After each trick, each player draws a card, winner first, to get back to three. The face-up trump card is drawn last.
Four players play in partnerships (sitting opposite) and may signal secretly.
scoring: After all cards are played, the player or team with 61 or more points wins. 60–60 is a draw. Often played best of three.
variations: Three players: remove one 2 so the deck divides evenly.

games.name: Scopa
equipment: A 40-card Italian deck, or a standard deck with the 8s, 9s and 10s removed (suits: coins = diamonds)
games.objective: Capture cards from the table by matching or adding up. First to 11 points wins.
quickStart: Goal: first to 11 points.
Capture table cards that match or add up to the card you play.
Clear the table for a scopa. Points for most cards, most coins, the 7 of coins and primiera.
setup: Card values: Ace 1, 2–7 face value, Jack (Fante) 8, Queen (Cavallo) 9, King (Re) 10.
Deal three cards to each player and four face up on the table.
gameplay: On your turn, play one card. If it equals the value of a table card, you must capture that card. If not, you may capture any group of table cards that adds up to its value.
If a single matching card is on the table, you must take it rather than a combination.
If you can’t capture, your card stays on the table.
Capturing every card on the table is a ‘scopa’ (sweep) and scores 1 point.
When hands are empty, deal three more each (none to the table). At the end, the last player to capture takes any remaining table cards — this doesn’t count as a scopa.
scoring: 1 point each for: most cards; most coins (diamonds); the 7 of coins (settebello); the best ‘primiera’ (for each suit, your best card counts: 7 = 21, 6 = 18, Ace = 16, 5 = 15, 4 = 14, 3 = 13, 2 = 12, face cards 10 — highest total wins); and 1 per scopa.
First to 11 points wins.
variations: Scopone: four players in partnerships, nine cards each and none on the table at the start.

games.name: Belote
equipment: A 32-card deck: A, K, Q, J, 10, 9, 8, 7 of each suit
Pen and paper or the score tracker
games.objective: The team that chooses trumps must take more points than the other team. First to 501 (or 1,000) wins.
quickStart: Goal: first partnership to 501.
Take the turned card or name trumps; trump Jack and 9 are the top cards.
The taking team must score more than the defenders, or lose everything.
setup: Four players in two partnerships, partners opposite.
Deal five cards each (three then two) and turn the next card face up.
gameplay: Bidding round 1: each player in turn may take the turned card, making its suit trumps, or pass. Round 2: a player may name a different suit as trumps, or pass. If all pass twice, redeal.
The taker adds the turned card to their hand and receives two more; everyone else receives three (eight cards each).

Declarations (shown during the first trick): sequences of 3 (20), 4 (50) or 5+ (100) in a suit; four Jacks (200), four 9s (150), four Aces, 10s, Kings or Queens (100). Only the team with the best declaration scores theirs.
Belote–Rebelote: holding K and Q of trumps scores 20, announced as you play them.

The player left of the dealer leads. You must follow suit. If you can’t, you must trump (overtrumping if possible) — unless your partner is currently winning the trick. When trumps are led you must play a higher trump if you can.
scoring: Card points total 152, plus 10 for the last trick (‘dix de der’) = 162.

If the taking team scores more than the defenders (counting declarations), each team scores its own points. If not, the taking team is ‘dedans’ (inside) and the defenders score all 162 plus all declarations.
Taking all eight tricks (‘capot’) scores 250 instead of 162.
First to 501 (or 1,000) wins.
variations: Coinche (Contrée): a bidding version with numeric contracts and doubling.
Klaverjas: the Dutch game, with similar card values and ‘roem’ bonuses.

games.name: Skat
equipment: A 32-card deck: A, K, Q, J, 10, 9, 8, 7 of each suit
Pen and paper or the score tracker
games.objective: Win the auction and, playing alone against the other two, take at least 61 of the 120 card points.
quickStart: Goal: as declarer, take 61 of 120 card points playing alone.
Bid by game value; the winner may use the two-card skat and chooses the game.
Jacks are always the top trumps. Win to score the game value; lose to pay double.
setup: Three active players (with four, the dealer sits out each hand). Deal ten cards each and two face down as the ‘skat’.
Card points: A 11, 10 10, K 4, Q 3, J 2; others 0. Total 120.
gameplay: Bidding uses game values (18, 20, 22, 23, 24, 27, 30 …). Middlehand bids to forehand (left of the dealer), who says ‘yes’ to hold or passes; then rearhand bids to the survivor. The winner becomes the declarer.
The declarer may pick up the skat and discard two cards (which count for them), or play ‘hand’ without it for a higher value.
The declarer chooses the game: a suit game (that suit is trumps), grand (only Jacks are trumps), or null (declarer must lose every trick, no trumps).
In suit and grand games the four Jacks are the highest trumps: J♣, J♠, J♥, J♦. Then, in a suit game, the trump suit ranks A, 10, K, Q, 9, 8, 7. Other suits rank A, 10, K, Q, 9, 8, 7.
Forehand leads. You must follow suit (the Jacks belong to the trump suit). If you can’t, play any card. The highest trump wins, otherwise the highest card of the suit led.
scoring: Game value = base value × multiplier. Base values: ♦ 9, ♥ 10, ♠ 11, ♣ 12, grand 24.
The multiplier is 1 + ‘matadors’ (how many top trumps in an unbroken run from J♣ the declarer has, or lacks), + 1 each for hand, schneider (90+ points), schwarz (all tricks) and announcing those.
Null games have fixed values: 23, hand 35, open 46, hand open 59.
If the declarer wins, they add the game value. If they lose, they subtract twice the game value. The game value must be at least the bid, or the declarer loses.
Play an agreed number of rounds (often a multiple of 3 or 4); highest total wins.
variations: Tournament scoring adds 50 points per game won and bonuses for opponents’ losses.

scorekeeper.hint: Use −1 or ±# when the declarer loses (twice the game value).

games.name: Rook
equipment: A Rook deck: cards 1–14 in four colours plus the Rook bird card (this game uses 5–14 and the Rook: 41 cards)
Pen and paper or the score tracker
games.objective: Partnerships bid for the right to choose trumps, then capture counting cards. This is the popular ‘Kentucky Discard’ form. First to 500 wins.
quickStart: Goal: first partnership to 500.
Bid for the nest and choose trumps; the Rook card is a trump.
Capture 5s, 10s, 14s and the Rook. Miss your bid and you lose it.
setup: Four players in two partnerships, partners opposite. Remove the 1s–4s.
Deal nine cards to each player and five face down to the ‘nest’.
Counting cards: each 5 is worth 5, each 10 and 14 is worth 10, the Rook is worth 20 (120 in total).
gameplay: Bidding: starting left of the dealer, players bid in multiples of 5 (commonly from 70) or pass; once passed you’re out.
The high bidder takes the nest, discards five cards, and names the trump colour.
The Rook is the lowest trump in standard rules (some play it highest) and counts as a trump. It may be played at any time, even if you could follow suit.
The player left of the dealer leads. Follow the colour led if you can; otherwise play any card. The highest trump wins, otherwise the highest card of the colour led.
Whoever wins the last trick also wins the nest’s counting cards.
scoring: Each side scores the counting cards it captured. If the bidding side fails to reach its bid, it loses the bid amount instead.
Many groups give 20 points for winning the most tricks.
First side to 500 wins.
variations: Full-deck Rook uses all 57 cards, with the 1 ranking high.
A standard deck can stand in: use A as 14, and a Joker for the Rook.

games.name: French Tarot
equipment: A French tarot deck (78 cards): four suits of 14 (K, Q, Cavalier, J, 10 … 1), 21 numbered trumps and the Excuse
Pen and paper or the score tracker
games.objective: The ‘taker’ plays alone against everyone else and must collect enough card points, depending on how many key cards (‘oudlers’) they capture.
quickStart: Goal: the taker must win enough card points against everyone else.
21 trumps plus the Excuse; you must trump if you can’t follow suit.
Points needed depend on how many oudlers (trump 1, trump 21, Excuse) you win.
setup: Four players is standard. Deal 18 cards each in threes, setting six cards aside one at a time as the ‘dog’ (chien).
Oudlers: trump 1 (le Petit), trump 21 and the Excuse.
gameplay: Bidding (lowest to highest): Petite (Prise), Garde, Garde sans le chien, Garde contre. Each player may bid higher than the last or pass. The highest bidder is the taker.

For Petite or Garde, the taker shows the dog, adds it to their hand and discards six (no Kings or trumps). For Garde sans, the dog counts for the taker unseen; for Garde contre, it counts for the defenders.
Player left of the dealer leads (play is counter-clockwise). Follow suit if you can. If you can’t, you must trump; and when trumps are played you must play a higher trump if you can.
The Excuse may be played at any time instead of following. It never wins the trick; its owner keeps it (and gives a low card in exchange).
The highest trump wins, otherwise the highest card of the suit led.
scoring: Card points: oudlers and Kings 4.5, Queens 3.5, Cavaliers 2.5, Jacks 1.5, all other cards 0.5 (91 in total).
The taker needs 56 points with no oudlers, 51 with one, 41 with two, 36 with three.
Score = (25 + the difference above or below the target) × multiplier (Petite 1, Garde 2, Garde sans 4, Garde contre 6). The taker wins or loses that amount from each defender.
Bonuses: Petit au bout (winning the last trick with the trump 1) 10 × multiplier; declared ‘handfuls’ of 10, 13 or 15 trumps; slam.
variations: Five players: the taker calls a King to choose a secret partner. Three players: 24 cards each.

scorekeeper.hint: Zero-sum: the taker gains (or loses) three times what each defender loses (or gains).

games.name: Yacht
equipment: Five six-sided dice
A score sheet with the 12 categories for each player
games.objective: Score the most points by filling each of 12 scoring categories once.
quickStart: Goal: highest total after filling all 12 categories.
Roll five dice up to three times, keeping any between rolls.
Score each turn in one empty category (sum of a number, full house, straights, Yacht = 50).
setup: Each player gets a score sheet column. Decide the order of play.
gameplay: On your turn, roll all five dice. You may then set aside any dice and re-roll the rest, up to two more times (three rolls in total).
After your last roll, you must write a score in one unused category — a zero if your dice don’t fit it.

Categories: Ones, Twos, Threes, Fours, Fives, Sixes (score the total of that number); Full House (three of a kind plus a pair: total of all dice); Four of a Kind (total of the four dice); Little Straight (1-2-3-4-5): 30; Big Straight (2-3-4-5-6): 30; Choice (any roll: total of all dice); Yacht (five of a kind): 50.
The game lasts 12 turns each.
scoring: Add up your categories. The highest total wins.
Solo: try to beat your best score.
variations: Yahtzee-style scoring (the familiar modern rules): 13 categories. Upper section: Ones to Sixes (total of that number), with a 35-point bonus if they add up to 63 or more. Lower section: Three of a Kind and Four of a Kind (total of all dice), Full House 25, Small Straight (four in a row) 30, Large Straight (five in a row) 40, Yahtzee (five of a kind) 50, Chance (total of all dice). Each extra five of a kind after scoring 50 in that box earns a 100 bonus.
Yatzy (Nordic): 15 categories, adding One Pair, Two Pairs and Three of a Kind, with a 50 bonus for 63+ in the upper section.

scorekeeper.hint: Full scorecard: Yahtzee-style, classic Yacht or Nordic Yatzy boxes, with bonuses worked out for you.

games.name: Generala
equipment: Five six-sided dice
A score sheet
games.objective: Score the most points by filling 10 categories — or win instantly with a Generala on your first roll.
quickStart: Goal: highest total after filling all categories.
Up to three rolls with five dice; score in one empty category each turn.
Straight 20, full 30, four of a kind 40, Generala 50. Generala on the first roll wins outright.
setup: Each player gets a score sheet column. Decide the order of play.
gameplay: On your turn, roll all five dice, then set aside any and re-roll the rest, up to three rolls in total.
After your last roll, score in one unused category (or cross one out with zero).
Number categories 1 to 6: the total of the dice showing that number.
Escalera (straight: 1-2-3-4-5, 2-3-4-5-6, or 3-4-5-6-1 in many rules): 20. Full (three of a kind plus a pair): 30. Poker (four of a kind): 40. Generala (five of a kind): 50.
Any of these four made on the first roll (‘servida’) scores 5 more.
A Generala served on the very first roll of a turn wins the game outright.
scoring: After everyone has filled every category, the highest total wins.
Some rules add a Double Generala category worth 100.
variations: House rules differ on servida bonuses and whether 3-4-5-6-1 counts as a straight.

games.name: Farkle
equipment: Six six-sided dice
Pen and paper or the score tracker
games.objective: Be the first to 10,000 points by rolling scoring dice and knowing when to stop.
quickStart: Goal: first to 10,000 points.
Roll six dice, set aside scoring dice (1s, 5s, triples…), then bank or roll the rest.
Roll no scoring dice and you ‘Farkle’ — losing that turn’s points.
setup: Decide the order of play. Agree your scoring table (common values below).
gameplay: On your turn, roll all six dice. Set aside at least one scoring die or combination.
Then either bank the points you’ve built up this turn, or re-roll the remaining dice to try for more.
If a roll contains no scoring dice, that’s a ‘Farkle’: you lose all points from this turn and play passes.
Hot dice: if all six dice have scored, you may roll all six again and keep adding.

Common scores: each 1 = 100; each 5 = 50; three of a kind = 100 × the number (three 1s = 1,000); four of a kind = 1,000; five of a kind = 2,000; six of a kind = 3,000; 1-2-3-4-5-6 straight = 1,500; three pairs = 1,500.
Many groups require at least 500 in one turn before you can bank your first points.
scoring: First to reach 10,000 triggers the end. Every other player gets one last turn to beat them. The highest score wins.
Solo: count how many turns you need to reach 10,000.
variations: Scoring tables vary a lot (e.g. four of a kind = double three of a kind). Agree them before you start.

scorekeeper.hint: Game ends when someone reaches 10,000 — remember everyone else gets one last turn.

games.name: Pig (dice)
equipment: One six-sided die (two for the Two-Dice Pig variant)
Pen and paper or the score tracker
games.objective: Be the first to 100 points.
quickStart: Goal: first to 100 points.
Roll a die as often as you like, adding up your turn total.
Roll a 1 and you lose the turn total. Hold to bank it.
setup: Decide the order of play.
gameplay: On your turn, roll the die as many times as you like, adding each roll to a running turn total.
If you roll a 1, you lose the whole turn total and play passes.
At any time you may ‘hold’: add the turn total to your score and pass the die.
scoring: First to 100 wins. Some groups give every player an equal number of turns.
variations: Two-Dice Pig: roll two dice. A single 1 loses the turn total; double 1s wipe out your entire score.
Big Pig: doubles count double; double 1s score 25.

games.name: Liar’s Dice
equipment: Five six-sided dice and one cup per player
games.objective: Make believable bids about all the hidden dice, call out liars, and be the last player with dice.
quickStart: Goal: be the last player with dice.
Roll hidden dice, then bid how many of a face are on the whole table — or call ‘Liar!’.
Wrong call or false bid loses a die.
setup: Each player has five dice and a cup. Everyone shakes their dice under their cup and peeks at their own dice only.
gameplay: The first player bids a quantity and a face for all dice on the table, e.g. ‘four 3s’ — meaning at least four dice in total show 3.
In turn, each player must either raise the bid — a higher quantity of any face, or the same quantity of a higher face — or challenge by calling ‘Liar!’ (or ‘Dudo’).
On a challenge, everyone reveals their dice. If there are at least as many of that face as bid, the challenger loses a die. If not, the bidder loses a die.
1s are wild in many rules and count as any face — except in bids on 1s themselves.
The player who lost a die starts the next round. Everyone re-rolls.
scoring: A player with no dice left is out. The last player with dice wins.
variations: Perudo: a bid on 1s may halve the quantity (rounded up); ‘Calza’ claims the bid is exactly right to win a die back.
Without wild 1s, the bidding is tighter.

scorekeeper.hint: Add 1 each time a player loses a die. Losing all five means they’re out.

games.name: Ship, Captain and Crew
equipment: Five six-sided dice
games.objective: Roll a 6 (ship), a 5 (captain) and a 4 (crew), in that order, then score as much ‘cargo’ as you can with the other two dice.
quickStart: Goal: roll a 6, 5 and 4 in that order, then score with the other two dice.
Three rolls with five dice; set aside ship (6), captain (5), crew (4).
The remaining two dice are your cargo score. Highest cargo wins.
setup: Decide the order of play.
gameplay: On your turn you get up to three rolls of the dice.

You must find a 6 first (the ship), then a 5 (the captain), then a 4 (the crew). Set each one aside as soon as you can, in order — if you roll 6 and 5 together you may keep both, but a 5 without a 6 can’t be kept.
Once you have ship, captain and crew, the other two dice are your cargo. If you still have rolls left, you may re-roll both cargo dice to try for a higher total.
If you don’t get all of ship, captain and crew within three rolls, you score nothing.
scoring: Your score is the cargo total (2–12). After everyone has played, the highest score wins the round. Ties roll off.
variations: Some groups let you re-roll just one cargo die.

games.name: Mexico
equipment: Two six-sided dice
Counters or coins for lives (e.g. 6 each)
games.objective: Avoid having the lowest roll each round, and be the last player with lives left.
quickStart: Goal: don’t have the lowest roll.
Two dice read as a number, higher first (5 and 3 = 53). 21 is Mexico, then doubles.
Lowest roll each round loses a life. Last with lives wins.
setup: Each player starts with the same number of lives (e.g. 6 counters).
gameplay: Read two dice as a two-digit number, with the higher die first: a 3 and a 5 is 53.
Ranking, highest first: 21 (‘Mexico’) beats everything; then doubles from 66 down to 11; then the rest from 65 down to 31.
In each round, the first player rolls up to three times, keeping only their last roll. The number of rolls they use is the maximum for everyone else that round.
After everyone has rolled, the player with the lowest roll loses a life. If a Mexico was rolled that round, the loser loses two lives.
The loser starts the next round.
scoring: A player with no lives left is out. The last player with a life wins.
variations: Mia (Mäxchen) is the bluffing version: you roll hidden, announce your roll, and the next player must beat it or call your bluff.

scorekeeper.hint: Add 1 (or 2 after a Mexico) to each round’s loser. Six means they’re out.

games.name: Chicago (dice)
equipment: Two six-sided dice
Pen and paper or the score tracker
games.objective: Score the most points over 11 rounds by rolling each round’s target total.
quickStart: Goal: most points over 11 rounds.
Round targets go from 2 to 12; roll two dice once each round.
Hit the round’s number to score it.
setup: Decide the order of play. There are 11 rounds, with targets 2, 3, 4 … up to 12.
gameplay: In each round, every player rolls both dice once.
If your total equals the round’s target number, you score that many points (e.g. rolling 7 in round 7 scores 7).
Otherwise you score nothing that round.
scoring: After round 12 (the eleventh round), the highest total wins.
variations: Some groups give each player as many rolls as they like until they miss.

scorekeeper.hint: Use ±# for 8–12.

games.name: Bunco
equipment: Three six-sided dice per table (four players per table)
Score sheets and a bell for the head table
games.objective: A social party game: score points with partners by rolling each round’s target number, and win the most rounds (and Buncos).
quickStart: Goal: score points with your partner and win the most rounds.
Roll three dice; score 1 per die showing the round number, and keep rolling while you score.
Three of the round number is a Bunco (21). Head table ends the round at 21.
setup: Ideally 12 players at three tables of four; partners sit opposite each other. One table is the ‘head table’.
There are six rounds; the target number is the round number (round 1 = 1s, and so on).
gameplay: At each table, players take turns rolling three dice. Score 1 point for each die showing the target number, and keep rolling as long as you score.
Three of the target number is a ‘Bunco’: 21 points (and shout ‘Bunco!’).
Three of a kind of any other number scores 5 points (in many rules).
When a turn scores nothing, the dice pass to the left. Points go to your partnership.
The round ends when a team at the head table reaches 21 points; they ring the bell and everyone stops.
Winning teams move up a table (head-table winners stay) and partners change before the next round.
scoring: Each player records wins and losses for each round, and Buncos rolled.
Prizes traditionally go to most wins, most Buncos, most losses and so on.
variations: Rules for moving tables, partner changes and prizes vary between groups.

scorekeeper.hint: Track each player’s round wins (or Buncos).

games.name: Shut the Box
equipment: A Shut the Box board with tiles numbered 1–9 (or paper with the numbers 1–9 to cross off)
Two six-sided dice
games.objective: Close (‘shut’) as many numbered tiles as possible, ideally all of them.
quickStart: Goal: shut as many numbered tiles (1–9) as you can.
Roll two dice and shut tiles that add up to the total.
Can’t match the roll? Your score is the tiles left open — lowest wins.
setup: Open all the tiles 1–9.
gameplay: Roll both dice. Shut any combination of open tiles that adds up to the total (e.g. a roll of 8 can shut 8, or 5+3, or 1+2+5).
Keep rolling and shutting tiles.
Common rule: once tiles 7, 8 and 9 are all shut, you may choose to roll just one die.
Your turn ends when you can’t shut tiles matching your roll.
scoring: Your score is the total of the tiles still open (lower is better). Shutting every tile (‘shutting the box’) wins immediately.
Play several rounds; the lowest total wins. Solo: try to shut the box.
variations: Some pub versions read the open tiles as digits (e.g. 1, 3, 4 open scores 134).

scorekeeper.hint: Add the total of the tiles left open each round.

games.name: Spite and Malice
equipment: Two standard 52-card decks with different backs, plus four jokers (optional)
games.objective: Be the first to get rid of your pay-off pile by playing its cards onto shared centre stacks built from Ace to Queen.
quickStart: Goal: be first to empty your pay-off pile.
Build shared centre stacks from Ace to Queen; Kings are wild.
Play from your hand, pay-off pile and discard piles; end each turn with a discard.
setup: Shuffle one deck (no jokers) and deal 20 cards face down to each player as their pay-off pile. Turn each player’s top pay-off card face up. Set the rest of that deck aside.
Shuffle the other deck (with any jokers) together with the leftover cards to form the stock. Deal five cards to each player’s hand.
Leave space in the middle for centre stacks, and in front of each player for four personal discard piles.
gameplay: Centre stacks are started with an Ace and built upward regardless of suit: A, 2, 3 … up to Queen. Kings (and jokers) are wild and can stand for any card except an Ace in most rules.
At the start of your turn, draw from the stock until you have five cards in hand.

Play as many cards as you can to the centre stacks — from your hand, from the top of your pay-off pile, or from the top of any of your discard piles. When you play your top pay-off card, turn up the next one.
If you empty your hand during your turn, draw five more and carry on.
End your turn by placing one card from your hand face up on one of your four discard piles. Discard piles can’t be played onto by anyone else.
When a centre stack reaches the Queen, it is shuffled into the stock.
scoring: The first player to play the last card of their pay-off pile wins.
Optional scoring: the winner scores 5 points per card left in the opponents’ pay-off piles; play to an agreed total.
variations: Pay-off piles of 26 or 30 cards make a longer game.
Some rules require discards to go on a pile only if they are the same rank or one lower than its top card.
Skip-Bo is a commercial version played with a special numbered deck (1–12 plus Skip-Bo wild cards).

games.name: Balut
equipment: Five six-sided dice
A score sheet with seven categories, each with four boxes
games.objective: Score the highest total by filling each of seven categories four times — a longer, more tactical cousin of Yacht.
quickStart: Goal: highest total after filling seven categories four times each.
Up to three rolls with five dice, scoring in one empty box each turn.
Fours, Fives, Sixes, Straight, Full House, Choice and Balut (five of a kind).
setup: Each player gets a score sheet. There are 28 turns each: seven categories × four boxes.
gameplay: On your turn, roll all five dice, then set aside any and re-roll the rest, up to three rolls in total.
After your last roll, write a score in an empty box of any category (a zero if the dice don’t fit).
Fours, Fives, Sixes: the total of the dice showing that number.
Straight: 1-2-3-4-5 scores 15; 2-3-4-5-6 scores 20.
Full House (three of a kind plus a pair): total of all dice.
Choice: total of all dice (any roll).
Balut (five of a kind): 20 plus the total of the dice.
scoring: Simple scoring: after 28 turns, the highest total wins.
Traditional scoring converts results to bonus points — for example for high category totals (such as 52+ in Fours) or filling every Straight box — so check the sheet you’re using.
variations: Solo: play all 28 turns and try to beat your best total.

games.name: Going to Boston
equipment: Three six-sided dice
games.objective: Get the highest three-dice total by keeping your best die after each roll.
quickStart: Goal: highest total of three dice.
Roll three, keep the highest; roll two, keep the highest; roll the last one.
Add up the three kept dice. Highest wins the round.
setup: Decide the order of play.
gameplay: Roll all three dice and set aside the highest one.
Roll the other two dice and set aside the higher one.
Roll the last die.
Your score is the total of the three dice you kept (3 to 18).
scoring: After everyone has had a turn, the highest score wins the round. Ties roll off. Play several rounds and count wins.
variations: Multiplication: multiply the kept die values instead of adding (e.g. 6 × 6 × 5 = 180).

games.name: Blitz
equipment: One standard 52-card deck, no jokers
Three coins or counters per player (lives)
games.objective: Collect three cards of one suit totalling as close to 31 as possible. The lowest hand each round loses a life.
quickStart: Goal: get your three cards of one suit as close to 31 as possible.
Each turn, draw from the stock or discard pile, then discard one — or knock to end the round.
Lowest hand loses a life; hit 31 exactly and everyone else loses one.
setup: Each player starts with three lives (coins or counters).
Deal three cards to each player. Turn the next card face up to start the discard pile; the rest is the stock.
Card values: Ace 11, court cards 10, others face value. Only cards of the same suit add together.
gameplay: On your turn, take the top card of the stock or the discard pile, then discard one card face up.
Your hand’s value is the total of your best suit (e.g. A♥ K♥ 4♠ = 21).
Instead of drawing, you may knock if you think your hand will beat at least one other player. Everyone else gets one more turn, then all hands are shown.
If you are dealt or draw exactly 31 (Ace plus two 10-value cards in one suit), show it immediately — the round ends and every other player loses a life.
Three of a kind is worth 30½ in many rules.
scoring: After a knock, the player with the lowest hand loses a life. If the knocker is lowest, they lose two lives.
A player with no lives left is out (some allow one last round ‘on the bus’). The last player with a life wins.
variations: Some groups count three of a kind as 30, or don’t count it at all.
Ties for lowest: all tied players lose a life, unless one of them is the knocker.

scorekeeper.hint: Add 1 to each round’s loser (2 for a failed knock). Three means they’re out.

games.name: GOPS
equipment: One standard 52-card deck, no jokers
games.objective: Win the most points by bidding cards from your hand for prize cards, in secret and at the same time.
quickStart: Goal: win the most prize points.
A prize card is turned up; both players bid one card from their hand face down, then reveal.
Higher bid takes the prize. Every card is used once, so plan your bids.
setup: Take out the diamonds, shuffle them and place them face down as the prize pile.
One player takes all the hearts, the other all the spades (a third player can take the clubs). Clubs are set aside in a two-player game.
Values: Ace 1, 2–10 face value, Jack 11, Queen 12, King 13.
gameplay: Turn up the top prize card.
Each player secretly chooses one card from their hand as a bid and places it face down. Reveal the bids together.
The higher bid wins the prize card. Bid cards are discarded — each can be used only once.
If the bids are equal, the prize is discarded (or, in a common rule, carried over to the next prize).
Continue until all 13 prizes have been played.
scoring: Add up the values of the prize cards you won (91 in total). Highest total wins.
variations: Three players: the third player takes the clubs. The highest bid wins; if the two highest bids tie, nobody wins that prize.

games.name: Ranter-Go-Round
equipment: One standard 52-card deck, no jokers
Three counters or coins per player (lives)
games.objective: Don’t be the player holding the lowest card at the end of each round.
quickStart: Goal: don’t hold the lowest card when everyone reveals.
Everyone gets one card. In turn, keep it or swap with the player on your left (a King can’t be taken).
Lowest card loses a life; last player with lives wins.
setup: Each player has three lives.
Deal one card face down to each player. Aces are low, Kings high.
gameplay: Starting left of the dealer, each player may keep their card or demand to swap it with the player on their left.
A player holding a King can refuse the swap by showing it (‘King!’), and the turn passes on.
The dealer goes last and may swap their card with the top card of the deck instead.
Everyone reveals their card.
scoring: The player (or players) with the lowest card loses a life.
Players with no lives left drop out; the last player standing wins.
variations: Some groups play that a swapped-out card can’t be passed back, or that anyone passed a King must reveal it.

games.name: Big Two
equipment: One standard 52-card deck, no jokers
games.objective: Be the first to get rid of all your cards by beating each play with a higher combination.
quickStart: Goal: be first to play out all 13 cards.
Beat the last play with a higher single, pair, triple or five-card poker hand — or pass.
When everyone passes, the last player to play leads anything.
setup: Deal 13 cards to each of four players (with three, deal 17 each and the holder of the extra card starts).
Ranks, low to high: 3, 4, 5 … K, A, 2. Suits break ties: ♦ (lowest), ♣, ♥, ♠ (highest).
gameplay: The player with the 3♦ starts and must include it in their first play.
Legal plays: a single card, a pair, three of a kind, or a five-card hand — straight, flush, full house, four of a kind plus any card, or straight flush (ranked in that order).
Each player in turn must play the same kind and number of cards, but higher, or pass. Passing doesn’t stop you playing later in the same round.
When everyone else passes, the last player to play clears the pile and leads anything.
scoring: When someone goes out, every other player scores penalty points: 1 per card left, doubled with 10 or more cards, tripled with 13.
Lowest total after an agreed number of deals (or when someone passes a limit) wins.
variations: Some groups let a 2 be part of straights only as the top card, or rank flushes by suit before rank.

games.name: Tiến Lên
equipment: One standard 52-card deck, no jokers
games.objective: Be the first to play all your cards, beating the previous play each time.
quickStart: Goal: be first to play out all 13 cards.
Beat the last play with the same type of combination, higher — or pass (and sit out until the pile clears).
2s are highest; ‘bombs’ such as four of a kind can beat 2s.
setup: Deal 13 cards to each player (with fewer than four, the rest are unused).
Ranks, low to high: 3, 4 … K, A, 2. Suits, low to high: ♠, ♣, ♦, ♥.
gameplay: In the first game the holder of the 3♠ leads it (alone or in a combination). Later games: the previous winner leads.
Combinations: single, pair, three of a kind, four of a kind, a sequence of three or more consecutive cards (2s can’t be in sequences), or a double sequence (three or more consecutive pairs).
Each player must beat the last play with the same type and number of cards, ranked higher by the highest card — or pass. Once you pass, you can’t play again until the pile is cleared.
When everyone else has passed, the last player to play leads anything.
Bombs: four of a kind or a double sequence of three pairs can beat a single 2; a double sequence of four pairs can beat a pair of 2s.
scoring: Players finish in order as they go out. A common scoring: 1st place 3 points, 2nd 2, 3rd 1, last 0. Play an agreed number of games.
variations: Southern and Northern Vietnamese rules differ (Northern requires following suit or colour). Some groups award an instant win for four 2s or six pairs.

games.name: James Bond
equipment: One standard 52-card deck, no jokers
games.objective: Be the first to turn all your piles into sets of four of a kind.
quickStart: Goal: make every one of your piles four of a kind.
Both play at once, swapping one card at a time with the four face-up cards in the middle.
Pick up only one pile at a time. First to finish shouts ‘James Bond!’.
setup: Two players: deal six face-down piles of four cards to each player and four cards face up in the middle.
Players may not look at their piles until play starts.
gameplay: On ‘Go!’ both players play at the same time.
Pick up any one of your piles. You may swap cards from it with the face-up cards in the middle, one card for one card.
Put the pile back face down before picking up another one. You may only ever hold one pile.
If nobody wants any of the middle cards, gather them, shuffle and deal them back face up.
When every one of your piles is a set of four, shout ‘James Bond!’.
scoring: The first player to correctly complete all their sets wins. A false call loses the round.
variations: Three players: deal four piles each, with four cards in the middle.

games.name: Escoba
equipment: A 40-card Spanish deck, or a standard deck with the 8s, 9s and 10s removed (coins = diamonds)
games.objective: Capture table cards that add up to 15 together with the card you play. First to 21 points wins.
quickStart: Goal: first to 21 points.
Play a card and capture table cards that make 15 together with it.
Clearing the table is an ‘escoba’ (1 point). Score for most cards, coins and 7s.
setup: Card values: Ace 1, 2–7 face value, Jack (Sota) 8, Queen (Caballo) 9, King (Rey) 10.
Deal three cards to each player and four face up on the table. If the four table cards total 15 (or 30), the dealer takes them as an escoba.
gameplay: On your turn, play one card. If it plus one or more table cards adds up to exactly 15, you may capture those cards along with your card.
If you can’t (or choose not to) capture, your card stays face up on the table.
Capturing every card on the table is an escoba, worth 1 point.
When hands are empty, deal three more each. After the last deal, the last player to capture takes any remaining table cards (not an escoba).
scoring: 1 point each for: most cards; most coins (diamonds); the 7 of coins; most 7s (all four 7s often score 2). Plus 1 per escoba.
First to 21 points wins (some play to 15).
variations: Scopa di Quindici is the Italian equivalent; Italian Scopa captures by matching or summing to the played card’s value instead.

games.name: Eleusis
equipment: Two standard 52-card decks shuffled together
Paper and pen for the dealer’s secret rule
games.objective: Work out the dealer’s secret rule for which cards may be played, and get rid of your cards by playing correctly.
quickStart: Goal: work out the secret rule and play legal cards.
The dealer writes a rule (e.g. ‘alternate red and black’). Play a card; the dealer says right or wrong.
Right cards build the main line; wrong cards go to the side and cost you penalty cards.
setup: One player is the dealer (‘God’) and secretly writes down a rule about which card may follow the previous one, e.g. ‘play a higher card or a card of the same suit’.
Deal 14 cards to each other player. Turn one card face up as the start of the main line.
gameplay: In turn, each player plays one card to the end of the main line.
If it follows the rule, the dealer says ‘right’ and it stays on the main line.
If not, the dealer says ‘wrong’; the card is placed below the main line where it was tried, and the player draws two penalty cards.

Instead of playing, a player who thinks they have no legal card may declare ‘no play’ and show their hand. If they’re right, their hand is reshuffled with fewer cards; if wrong, the dealer plays a legal card for them and they draw penalties.
Anyone may try to guess the rule at any time; the round ends when someone runs out of cards or the deck runs out.
scoring: Each player scores the difference between the most cards held by anyone and their own count; a player who went out gets a bonus.
The dealer scores based on how well-balanced the rule was (best when it was neither too easy nor too hard). Everyone deals once; highest total wins.
variations: Eleusis Express is a shorter, simpler version. The Prophet rule lets a player who thinks they know the rule take over judging plays for bonus points.

games.name: Cuttle
equipment: One standard 52-card deck, no jokers
games.objective: Be the first to have 21 points of number cards on your side of the table.
quickStart: Goal: be first to 21 points of cards in front of you.
Each turn: draw, play a number card for points, ‘scuttle’ an opponent’s card, or use a card’s special power.
Kings lower your target; Queens protect; Jacks steal; 8s reveal hands.
setup: Two players: deal 5 cards to the dealer and 6 to the other player, who goes first. The rest is the draw pile; a discard pile is the ‘scrap’.
gameplay: On your turn, do one of: draw a card; play an Ace–10 face up for points (Ace = 1); scuttle; play a one-off; or play a permanent.
Scuttle: discard one of your number cards to destroy an opponent’s number card of lower value (or equal value of lower suit: ♣ < ♦ < ♥ < ♠). Both go to the scrap.

One-offs (play then scrap): Ace — scrap all point cards; 2 — scrap a permanent, or counter a one-off; 3 — take any card from the scrap; 4 — opponent discards two cards; 5 — draw two; 6 — scrap all permanents; 7 — draw and immediately play the top card; 9 — return a permanent or point card to its owner’s hand.

Permanents: 8 (glasses) — opponent plays with their hand face up; Queen — your other cards can’t be targeted; King — reduces your target to 14, then 10, 7 and 5 with more Kings; Jack — steal an opponent’s point card.
Hand limit: 8 cards.
scoring: You win the moment your point cards total your target (21, lowered by Kings). If the deck runs out and three players in a row pass, it’s a draw.
variations: House rules vary for the 2 and 9; some play 8s as point cards too. Three- and four-player versions exist.

games.name: Double Solitaire
equipment: One standard 52-card deck per player, each with a different back
games.objective: Play the most cards from your own deck onto shared foundations.
quickStart: Goal: get the most of your cards onto the shared foundations.
Each player plays their own Klondike layout, taking turns.
Foundations in the middle are shared — anyone can build on them.
setup: Each player deals their own deck into a normal Klondike layout (seven piles of 1 to 7 cards, top card face up) with the rest as their stock.
Leave space in the middle for shared foundations — up to eight, two per suit, with two players.
gameplay: Players take turns. On your turn, make as many moves as you like within your own layout, and play cards to any foundation in the middle (Ace up in suit).
Your turn ends when you turn a card from your stock to your waste pile that you can’t (or don’t) play.
You may never move cards in another player’s layout.
scoring: When nobody can move, sort the foundations by card backs. Most cards played wins; clearing your whole layout wins outright.
variations: Real-time version: everyone plays at once (very close to Racing Demon / Nertz).

games.name: Cribbage Squares
equipment: One standard 52-card deck, no jokers
games.objective: Place 16 cards in a 4×4 grid to make eight high-scoring Cribbage hands.
quickStart: Goal: score 61+ from eight Cribbage hands.
Turn cards one at a time and place each in an empty square of a 4×4 grid.
Each row and column is a hand, scored with the 17th card as the starter.
setup: Shuffle the deck. You’ll fill a 4×4 grid, one card at a time.
gameplay: Turn up a card and place it in any empty square. Once placed, it can’t move.
Repeat until all 16 squares are filled.
Turn up the 17th card as the starter. (If it’s a Jack, score 2 for ‘his heels’.)

Score each of the four rows and four columns as a Cribbage hand together with the starter: fifteens 2, pairs 2, runs 1 per card, a four-card flush 4 (5 with the starter), and the Jack of the starter’s suit 1.
scoring: Add up all eight hands. Common targets: 61 to win, 121 as a great score.
variations: Cribbage Solitaire (non-grid): deal six cards, keep four, put two in your own crib, and score through the deck.

games.name: Écarté
equipment: A 32-card deck: K, Q, J, A, 10, 9, 8, 7 of each suit
games.objective: Win at least three of five tricks. First to 5 points wins.
quickStart: Goal: win 3 of 5 tricks; first to 5 points.
Before play, the non-dealer may propose swapping cards; the dealer accepts or refuses.
Follow suit and win the trick if you can. All five tricks scores 2.
setup: Cards rank K (high), Q, J, A, 10, 9, 8, 7 — the Ace is between Jack and 10.
Deal five cards each (in packets of 3 and 2). Turn the next card up for trumps; if it is a King, the dealer scores 1 point.
gameplay: The non-dealer may play with these cards or ‘propose’ an exchange. The dealer may accept or refuse.
If accepted, each player discards any number of cards and draws replacements, non-dealer first. The non-dealer may then propose again, and so on until someone refuses or the stock runs out.
A player holding the King of trumps may announce it before playing their first card, scoring 1 point.
The non-dealer leads. You must follow suit and must win the trick if you can; if you can’t follow suit, you must trump if you can.
scoring: Win 3 or 4 tricks: 1 point. Win all 5 (the ‘vole’): 2 points.
If a player refused an exchange (or played without proposing) and then fails to win 3 tricks, the opponent scores 2 instead of 1.
First to 5 points wins.
variations: Players often agree a limit on the number of exchanges.

games.name: Le Truc
equipment: A 32-card deck: 7, 8, A, K, Q, J, 10, 9 of each suit
Pen and paper or the score tracker
games.objective: Win two of three tricks — and bluff your opponent into folding when the stakes rise. First to 12 points wins.
quickStart: Goal: win 2 of 3 tricks; first to 12 points.
No trumps, no need to follow suit. Highest rank wins (7 is top).
Before playing a card you may raise the stakes; the opponent accepts, folds or raises.
setup: Cards rank 7 (high), 8, A, K, Q, J, 10, 9. Suits don’t matter.
Deal three cards to each player. A hand starts worth 1 point.
gameplay: The non-dealer leads. You don’t have to follow suit — the higher-ranked card wins the trick, whatever the suit.
If two cards tie, the trick is ‘spoiled’ and won by nobody; the same leader leads again.
Whoever wins two tricks (or one trick plus a spoiled one, or the first trick if the rest are spoiled) wins the hand.
Betting: before playing a card on your turn, you may offer to raise the hand’s value by 1. Your opponent must accept (play on for the new value), fold (you win the current value), or raise again.
Before the deal is played you may also ask for a new hand, if your opponent agrees.
scoring: The winner of a hand scores its value (1, or more if raised). First to 12 points wins a game; best of three games is a match.
variations: Rules vary by region: Parlett/McLeod and Sackson differ on spoiled tricks and how far stakes can rise. Four players play in partnerships.

games.name: Put
equipment: One standard 52-card deck, no jokers
games.objective: Win two of three tricks, or bluff your opponent into giving up. First to 5 points wins.
quickStart: Goal: first to 5 points.
Three cards each; win 2 tricks. 3 is the highest card, then 2, Ace, King…
Say ‘Put’ to challenge: if they accept, the hand wins the whole game; if they refuse, you score 1.
setup: Cards rank 3 (highest), 2, A, K, Q, J, 10, 9 … 4 (lowest). Suits don’t matter.
Deal three cards to each player.
gameplay: The non-dealer leads. No need to follow suit; the higher-ranked card wins. Equal cards tie and neither wins the trick.
Win two tricks (or one plus ties) to win the hand: 1 point.
At any time before or during play, either player may say ‘Put’. The other must accept or refuse.
If they refuse, the challenger scores 1 point and the hand ends. If they accept, whoever wins the hand wins the whole game.
scoring: First to 5 points wins — or the winner of an accepted ‘Put’.
variations: Before play, the non-dealer may ask for a new deal; the dealer either agrees or concedes 1 point.

games.name: Klaberjass
equipment: A 32-card deck: A, K, Q, J, 10, 9, 8, 7 of each suit
Pen and paper or the score tracker
games.objective: The player who chooses trumps must score more points than the opponent. First to 500 wins.
quickStart: Goal: first to 500.
Take the turned-up suit (or name another) as trumps — then you must outscore your opponent.
Trump Jack (20) and Nine (14) are the top cards. Sequences and K-Q of trumps score extra.
setup: Deal six cards each in threes and turn the next card face up as the proposed trump.
gameplay: Bidding: the non-dealer may ‘take’ (accept that suit as trumps), pass, or ‘schmeiss’ (offer to redeal). Then the dealer. If both pass, each in turn may name another suit as trumps. If both pass again, redeal.
Deal three more cards each. The holder of the trump 7 may swap it for the turned-up card.
Sequences: three in a row in one suit score 20, four or more score 50. Only the player with the best sequence scores theirs.
The non-dealer leads. You must follow suit and must trump if you can’t. If trumps are led you must play a higher trump if able.
Holding the King and Queen of trumps (‘Bella’) scores 20 when the second is played. Winning the last trick scores 10.
scoring: Each player scores their card points, sequences, Bella and last trick.
If the player who chose trumps scores less than the opponent, they are ‘bête’: the opponent scores both totals.
First to 500 wins.
variations: Belote (France) and Klaverjas (Netherlands) are the four-player partnership relatives; Jass is the Swiss family.

games.name: Honeymoon Bridge
equipment: One standard 52-card deck, no jokers
Score pad (or the score tracker)
games.objective: A two-player version of Bridge: build your hand in the first half, then bid and play a contract.
quickStart: Goal: score like Bridge with only two players.
First 13 tricks build your hand: winner takes the face-up stock card, loser the next one.
Then bid a contract and play the last 13 tricks.
setup: Deal 13 cards each. The remaining 26 form the stock; turn the top card face up.
gameplay: First half (no trumps, tricks don’t count): the non-dealer leads; follow suit if you can. The trick winner takes the face-up stock card and the loser takes the next card unseen. Turn up the next stock card.
When the stock is gone, each player holds 13 new cards.
Bidding: as in Bridge (levels 1–7 with suits or no trumps, double and redouble), between the two players.
Second half: play 13 tricks with the contract’s trumps, following suit if you can.
scoring: Use Bridge scoring (see Contract Bridge), with rubbers of two games.
variations: Several other two-handed Bridge versions exist, e.g. with dummy hands dealt face up (Double Dummy) or with a widow.

games.name: Sedma
equipment: A 32-card deck: A, K, Q, J, 10, 9, 8, 7 of each suit
games.objective: Capture Aces and 10s in tricks. A card can only be beaten by one of the same rank — or by a 7.
quickStart: Goal: capture the most Aces and 10s (10 points each).
Play any card. The trick goes to the last player who matched the led card’s rank or played a 7.
The leader may keep a trick going by playing another matching card or a 7.
setup: Suits and normal rank order don’t matter. Aces and 10s are worth 10 points each; the last trick is worth 10 (90 in total).
Deal four cards each (four players play in partnerships, partners opposite). The rest is the stock.
gameplay: The leader plays any card. Each other player plays any card in turn.
The trick is won by the last player who played a card of the same rank as the led card, or a 7 (sevens are wild). If nobody did, the leader wins it.
When the trick comes back to the leader and the leader’s side isn’t currently winning, the leader may continue it by playing another card of the led rank or a 7; the others then play again.
After each trick, everyone draws back up to four cards, starting with the trick winner, who leads next.
scoring: The side with more card points (over 45) wins the deal. Winning all eight tricks or all point cards often scores double. Play a set number of deals.
variations: Three players: deal from a deck with two 8s removed. Some groups count sevens as only able to beat non-point cards.

games.name: Jass
equipment: A 36-card deck: A, K, Q, J, 10, 9, 8, 7, 6 of each suit (or a Swiss Jass deck)
Pen and paper or the score tracker
games.objective: The national game of Switzerland. Partnerships take turns choosing trumps and race to an agreed total, usually 1,000 or 2,500.
quickStart: Goal: first partnership to the target (often 1,000).
The leader chooses trumps — or ‘shoves’ (schieben) the choice to partner. Trump Jack (20) and Nine (14) are top.
Score card points, declarations of sequences and sets, and King-Queen of trumps.
setup: Four players in two partnerships. Deal nine cards each.
Trumps rank J (‘Buur’, 20 points), 9 (‘Nell’, 14), A (11), K (4), Q (3), 10 (10), 8, 7, 6. Other suits rank A (11), K (4), Q (3), J (2), 10 (10), 9, 8, 7, 6. Last trick 5. Total 157.
gameplay: The player who leads first chooses trumps — or says ‘schieben’ and their partner must choose. Options: a trump suit, ‘Obenabe’ (no trumps, high cards win) or ‘Undenufe’ (no trumps, low cards win; then the 6 scores 11).
Follow suit if you can, but you may always trump instead. The trump Jack never has to follow trumps. You may not undertrump unless you have only trumps.

Declarations (‘Weis’) in the first trick: sequences of 3 cards 20, 4 cards 50, 5 or more 100; four Jacks 200, four 9s 150, four of A, K, Q or 10 100. Only the partnership with the best declaration scores all of theirs.
‘Stöck’: holding King and Queen of trumps scores 20.
scoring: Each team scores its card points plus declarations. Winning all nine tricks (‘Match’) scores 257. First team to the agreed total wins.
variations: Swiss Jass has dozens of regional forms (Differenzler, Coiffeur, Molotov); Schieber is the most common.

games.name: Briscola Chiamata
equipment: A 40-card Italian deck, or a standard deck with the 8s, 9s and 10s removed
games.objective: The auction winner calls a card to choose a secret partner. Together they need more than 60 of the 120 card points.
quickStart: Goal: the caller’s team needs 61+ of 120 points.
Bid by card rank (Ace, 3, King… down to 2); the winner names a suit — whoever holds that card is their secret partner.
That suit is trumps. No need to follow suit.
setup: Cards rank A, 3, K, Q, J, 7, 6, 5, 4, 2. Points: Ace 11, 3 10, King 4, Queen 3, Jack 2.
Deal eight cards to each of the five players.
gameplay: Auction: players bid ranks in descending order (‘Ace’, ‘Three’, ‘King’ … ‘Two’), each lower than the last, or pass. Below ‘Two’ you can bid points needed above 61 instead.
The winner names a suit. The card of that suit and the bid rank is the ‘called card’; its holder is the secret partner, revealed only when the card is played. That suit is trumps.
The player left of the dealer leads. No need to follow suit; highest trump wins, otherwise highest card of the suit led.
scoring: If the caller’s side takes 61 or more, the caller scores +2, the partner +1 and each opponent −1. If not, reversed (caller −2, partner −1, opponents +1). Payments often double for raised bids or a clean sweep.
variations: The caller may call a card in their own hand to play alone, for double stakes.

scorekeeper.hint: Use −1 / ±# for losing players — scores are zero-sum.

games.name: Doppelkopf
equipment: A 48-card deck: two each of A, 10, K, Q, J, 9 in every suit (or two standard decks, using 9s to Aces)
Pen and paper or the score tracker
games.objective: The two players holding the Queens of Clubs (team ‘Re’) secretly play against the other two (‘Kontra’). Re needs 121 of 240 points.
quickStart: Goal: your secret team takes most of the 240 card points (Re needs 121).
Holders of the two Q♣ are partners — but nobody says who they are.
Queens, Jacks, diamonds and the 10♥ are all trumps.
setup: Deal 12 cards to each of four players.
Trumps (high to low): 10♥, Q♣, Q♠, Q♥, Q♦, J♣, J♠, J♥, J♦, A♦, 10♦, K♦, 9♦. Of two identical cards, the first played wins.
Plain suits rank A, 10, K, 9 (hearts have no 10). Card points: A 11, 10 10, K 4, Q 3, J 2, 9 0.
gameplay: The player left of the dealer leads. Follow suit if you can (trumps count as one suit); otherwise play anything.
Teams reveal themselves through play — or by announcing ‘Re’ or ‘Kontra’ early, which doubles the stakes.
A player holding both Q♣ may announce a ‘Hochzeit’ (marriage) and partner with the first player to win a trick, or play a solo.
scoring: The winning team scores 1 game point, plus 1 each if the losers took under 90, under 60, under 30 or no tricks, plus 1 for beating the Q♣ team as Kontra. Announcements add to the value.
Each winner scores the total; each loser loses it. Play an agreed number of deals.
variations: Many groups play with the 9s removed (40 cards), and add extra points for capturing a ‘Fox’ (A♦) or winning the last trick with a ‘Charlie’ (J♣).

scorekeeper.hint: Zero-sum: winners gain what losers lose.

games.name: Ninety-Nine (trick-taking)
equipment: A 36-card deck: A, K, Q, J, 10, 9, 8, 7, 6 of each suit
Pen and paper or the score tracker
games.objective: Bid exactly how many tricks you’ll win — using three of your own cards as the bid. First to 100 points wins. (David Parlett’s classic three-player game.)
quickStart: Goal: first to 100 points.
Each player puts 3 cards face down as their bid: ♣ = 3 tricks, ♥ = 2, ♠ = 1, ♦ = 0.
Play the other 9 cards as tricks. 1 point per trick, plus a bonus if you make your bid exactly.
setup: Deal 12 cards to each of three players. Cards rank A (high) to 6.
Trumps for the first deal are agreed (commonly none or clubs). In many rules, the number of players who made their bid in one deal sets trumps for the next.
gameplay: Bidding: each player chooses three cards from their hand and places them face down as their bid. Each card’s suit counts: clubs 3, hearts 2, spades 1, diamonds 0. Total = tricks you’re bidding (0–9).
A player may ‘declare’ (show their bid cards to everyone) or ‘reveal’ (play with their whole hand face up) for higher bonuses.
Play nine tricks with the remaining cards. Follow suit if you can; highest trump wins, otherwise highest of the suit led.
Then turn the bid cards over and compare.
scoring: 1 point for each trick won.
Bonus for making your bid exactly: 30 if you’re the only one to do so, 20 each if two players do, 10 each if all three do.
Declaring adds 30 (if made; lose 30 if not); revealing adds 60. First to 100 wins.
variations: Four-player version uses a 52-card deck with three bid cards from 13. Not to be confused with the adding game Ninety-Nine.

games.name: Watten
equipment: A 32-card deck: A, K, Q, J, 10, 9, 8, 7 of each suit (traditionally German-suited: hearts = hearts, bells = diamonds, acorns = clubs, leaves = spades; Over = Queen, Under = Jack)
Pen and paper or the score tracker
games.objective: Win three of five tricks — and use bets and bluffs to raise the stakes or scare the other team off. First team to 11 points wins.
quickStart: Goal: first team to 11 points; win 3 of 5 tricks each hand.
Forehand picks a trump rank, the dealer picks a trump suit. K♥, 7♦ and 7♣ are always the top three cards.
No need to follow suit. Say ‘Go!’ to raise the stakes; the other team folds or plays on.
setup: Four players in partnerships, partners opposite. Deal five cards each (3 then 2); the rest are not used.

The three ‘Kritische’ are permanent top trumps: K♥ (Maxi), then 7♦ (Belli), then 7♣ (Spitz). If the card at the bottom of the cut is a Kritisch, the cutter may take it (then the dealer if the next is one too).
Forehand (dealer’s left) looks at their cards and names the trump rank (the ‘Schlag’), e.g. ‘tens’. Then the dealer names the trump suit. Only then may the other two pick up their cards.
gameplay: Trump order: the three Kritische; then the card of both trump suit and trump rank (the ‘Rechte’); then the other cards of the trump rank (equal — the first played wins); then the rest of the trump suit A, K, Q, J, 10, 9, 8, 7. Other suits rank A, K, Q, J, 10, 9, 8, 7.
Forehand leads. There is usually no need to follow suit — play any card. Highest trump wins, otherwise the highest card of the suit led.
Exception: if the Rechte is led to the first trick, the leader may call ‘Trumps or Kritisch’, and others must play one of those if they can.
As soon as a team wins three tricks the hand ends.

Betting: at any time a player may say ‘Go!’ to raise the hand from 2 to 3 points. The other team either gives up (the bettors score the current value) or plays on. Teams must alternate raises (4, 5 …).
Partners may use traditional secret signals (winks, lip movements) to show their best cards — part of the fun.
scoring: Winning a hand scores 2 points, or more if raised. First team to 11 wins.
Common rule: a team on 9 or 10 points (‘gespannt’) may not raise, and the hand counts 2 for them.
variations: Tyrolean Watten uses the 6♦ as a wild ‘Weli’ and plays to 15 or 18.
Blind Watten (South Tyrol): trumps are chosen secretly, and only the choosers’ partners are told by signals.
Two- and three-player versions exist.

games.name: Twenty
equipment: One standard 52-card deck, no jokers
Pen and paper or the score tracker
games.objective: Play cards that make each number from 1 up to 20 in turn, and keep your penalty points low. (A modern adding game by Brian Stovel, 2009, published on Pagat.com.)
quickStart: Goal: fewest penalty points; game ends at 100.
The count goes 1, 2, 3 … 20. On your turn, play cards that add up exactly to the count — or draw a card.
Kings are wild. Cards left in hand when someone goes out (or reaches 20) are penalties.
setup: Deal seven cards to each player. The rest is a face-down stack.
Values for making the count: Ace 1, 2–9 face value, 10/J/Q 10 (a pair of 10s, Jacks or Queens may count 10 instead of 20), King any number from 1 to 20.
gameplay: The count starts at 1. The player after the dealer begins.
On your turn, either draw one card, or ‘make the count’ by playing one card or a set of cards adding up exactly to the current number. Drawing is always allowed, even if you could play.
Each time the count is made, it goes up by one. It may take several turns before someone makes it.
The hand ends when a player plays their last card, or the count of 20 is made.
scoring: Penalties for cards left in hand: Ace–9 = 5 each, 10/J/Q = 10 each, King = 20.
Two players: when someone reaches 100, the lower total wins. With 3–4 players, play to 200.
variations: For more rules and tips see the game’s page on Pagat.com.

equipment: A 36-card deck: remove the 2s, 3s, 4s and 6s from a standard deck
Pen and paper or the score tracker
games.objective: Partnerships bid how many card points they’ll take, then capture Aces, 10s and 5s. First team to 200 wins.
quickStart: Goal: first partnership to 200.
Bid the card points your team will take (50–100, in fives); the winner names trumps.
Aces and 10s are worth 10, 5s are worth 5. Miss your bid and you lose it.
setup: Four players in partnerships, partners opposite.
Cards rank A, K, Q, J, 10, 9, 8, 7, 5. Point cards: each Ace 10, each 10 10, each 5 5 (100 in total).
Deal nine cards each, in threes.
gameplay: Bidding: starting left of the dealer, bid a multiple of 5 from 50 to 100, each bid higher than the last, or pass (once you pass you’re out). If everyone passes, redeal.
The highest bidder names trumps and leads the first card.
Follow suit if you can; otherwise play anything (you don’t have to trump). Highest trump wins, otherwise the highest card of the suit led.
scoring: If the bidding team took at least its bid, it scores all the card points it took; otherwise it loses the amount bid. Scores can go below zero (‘in the box’).
The other team scores its card points — except that a team already on 100 or more scores only if one of them bid.
First team to 200 wins; if both get there on the same hand, the bidders win. A team at −200 loses.
variations: With a 40-card deck (adding the 6s) and a four-card kitty taken by the bidder.
Some play to 300 or 500. Rook is a close relative with special cards.

scorekeeper.hint: Use −1 / ±# when the bidders fail their bid.

games.name: Swoop
equipment: Two decks with jokers for 3–4 players, three for 5–6, four for 7–8
Pen and paper or the score tracker
games.objective: Be the first to get rid of all your cards — hand, face-up and face-down — by playing equal or lower cards. A newer cousin of Palace.
quickStart: Goal: first to play out every card; others score what they hold.
Play 1–4 equal cards that are the same or lower than the pile. Play higher and you must pick up the pile first.
Four equal on top, a 10 or a joker ‘swoops’ the pile away and you go again.
setup: Each player takes 19 cards. Without looking, place four face down, then four face up on top of them. The other 11 are your hand.
Cards rank A (low), 2 … 9, J, Q, K (high). 10s and jokers are special.
gameplay: On your turn, play one to four cards of the same rank, from your hand and/or your face-up table cards.
If they are equal to or lower than the top of the pile, they go on the pile. If they are higher, you must first pick up the whole pile, then your cards start a new pile.
Swoop: if the top four cards of the pile are the same rank, or you play a 10 or a joker, the pile is removed from the game and you take another turn.
A face-down card can only be played as the first card of a turn: flip it and play it (plus any matching cards) with the usual consequences.
The first player out of cards — including their face-down cards — ends the deal.
scoring: Everyone else scores the cards they still hold: Ace 1, 2–9 face value, J/Q/K 10, 10s and jokers 50.
When someone reaches 500, the lowest total wins.
variations: Simpler scoring: Ace–9 = 5, J/Q/K = 10, 10s and jokers = 50.

games.name: Twenty-Nine
equipment: A 32-card deck: J, 9, A, 10, K, Q, 8, 7 of each suit
Spare low cards as hidden trump markers (optional)
games.objective: Partnerships bid how many card points they’ll win, with a trump suit kept secret until someone can’t follow suit. First team to +6 game points wins.
quickStart: Goal: first partnership to +6 game points.
Bid after seeing 4 cards; the winner secretly picks trumps. Jacks (3), 9s (2), Aces and 10s (1) are the point cards.
Trumps are revealed only when someone can’t follow suit.
setup: Four players in partnerships, partners opposite.
Every suit ranks J, 9, A, 10, K, Q, 8, 7. Points: Jacks 3, Nines 2, Aces 1, Tens 1 — 28 in all (29 with a point for the last trick).
Deal four cards each.
gameplay: Bidding: starting left of the dealer, bid a number of points from 15 to 28 or pass, until three pass in a row. If all others pass, the dealer must bid 15.
The winner secretly chooses trumps, placing a marker card of that suit face down. Then deal four more each (eight in all).
Left of the dealer leads; follow suit if you can. The first player who can’t follow suit asks for trumps to be revealed; from that trick on, the highest trump wins.

Royals: a player holding the King and Queen of trumps may declare them after their side wins a trick once trumps are known — it lowers their side’s target by 4 (or raises the bidders’ target by 4 if declared by an opponent).
scoring: If the bidding side took at least their bid (adjusted for Royals), they gain 1 game point; if not, they lose 1. The other side’s score doesn’t change.
First team to +6 wins; a team at −6 loses.
variations: Many regional versions: doubling and redoubling, a ‘single hand’ bid to win every trick, and counter-clockwise play are common.

scorekeeper.hint: Use −1 when the bidders fail.

games.name: Dou Dizhu
equipment: One standard 52-card deck plus two distinguishable jokers (54 cards)
games.objective: The ‘landlord’ plays alone against two peasants. Be first to get rid of all your cards by beating each play.
quickStart: Goal: be first out of cards — the landlord against the two peasants.
Bid 1–3 to be landlord (you get the 3 extra cards). Beat each play with a higher one of the same type, or pass.
Four of a kind is a bomb and two jokers a rocket — they beat anything and double the stakes.
setup: Cards rank (high to low): red joker, black joker, 2, A, K, Q … 3. Suits don’t matter.
Deal 17 cards each; leave three face down.
gameplay: Auction: players bid 1, 2 or 3 (each higher than the last) or pass. The highest bidder becomes the landlord and takes the three extra cards.

The landlord leads any single card or combination: pair, triple, triple with a single or pair attached, sequence of 5+ cards (3 to Ace), sequence of 3+ pairs, sequence of triples (with or without attachments), four with two attachments.
Each player in turn must beat the last play with the same type and number of cards, higher, or pass. Passing doesn’t stop you playing later.
Bomb (four of a kind) beats any combination except a higher bomb or the rocket; rocket (both jokers) beats everything.
When two players pass in a row, the last player to play leads anything.
scoring: If the landlord goes out first, each peasant pays them the bid; if a peasant goes out first, the landlord pays each peasant the bid.
Each bomb or rocket played doubles the payment.
variations: Four-player version uses two decks; many apps add extra doubling rules (e.g. ‘spring’ when the other side never plays a card).

scorekeeper.hint: Zero-sum: use −1 / ±# for losing players.

games.name: Jhyap
equipment: One standard 52-card deck plus two jokers (two decks for 4+ players)
Pen and paper or the score tracker
games.objective: Get the total of your hand as low as possible, then call ‘Yaniv!’ (or ‘Jhyap!’) when you think it’s the lowest at the table.
quickStart: Goal: keep your score low; over 200 and you’re out.
Each turn: throw away one card, a set or a run, then pick up one card.
With 5 or less in hand you may call ‘Yaniv!’ — but if anyone matches or beats you, you take a penalty.
setup: Card values: Ace 1, 2–10 face value, J/Q/K 10, Joker 0.
Deal five cards each. Turn the top of the stock face up to start the dump pile.
gameplay: On your turn, either call ‘Yaniv’ (see below) or throw then pick up.
Throw: one card, a set of two or more equal cards, or a run of three or more consecutive cards in one suit (Ace low; jokers can fill gaps).
Then pick up one card: the top of the stock, or the first or last card of the previous player’s throw.
Calling: at the start of your turn, if your hand totals 5 or less, you may call. Everyone shows their cards.
scoring: If the caller has the lowest total, they score 0 and everyone else scores their hand total.
If anyone has an equal or lower total, the caller scores 30 plus their hand (‘Asaf’), and everyone else scores their hand.
Over 200 points and you’re out; the last player in wins. Landing on exactly 100 drops you to 50, and exactly 200 to 100.
variations: Nepalese Jhyap and Dutch Kluft differ in the calling limit and penalties.

games.name: Ulti
equipment: A 32-card deck: A, 10, K, Q, J, 9, 8, 7 of each suit (traditionally Hungarian cards: Over = Queen, Under = Jack)
Pen and paper or the score tracker
games.objective: The national card game of Hungary. Bid for contracts — such as winning the last trick with the 7 of trumps — and play them alone against the other two.
quickStart: Goal: win the contract you bid, playing alone against two.
Bidding passes a 2-card talon round: pick it up, discard two, name a higher contract.
Contracts include Parti, Ulti (last trick with the trump 7), 40-100, Betli and Durchmars. Hearts score double.
setup: Deal 12 cards to the player on the dealer’s right and 10 to each of the others (play is anticlockwise).
With trumps, cards rank A, 10, K, Q, J, 9, 8, 7. Without trumps: A, K, Q, J, 10, 9, 8, 7.
Aces and 10s won in tricks are worth 10 each, and the last trick 10 (90 in all). Holding King and Queen of a suit adds 20, or 40 in trumps.
gameplay: Auction: the player with 12 cards discards two face down as the talon and names a contract. Each later bidder may pick up the talon, discard two, and name a higher contract. It ends when everyone in turn declines the talon.

Main contracts: Parti (simple game: take more card points than the opponents); Ulti (win the last trick with the 7 of trumps); 40-100 (take 100 points using the trump marriage); 20-100; Durchmars (win every trick); Betli (no trumps, lose every trick). Contracts can be combined, e.g. ‘Ulti with Parti’.
The bidder names trumps and leads. Follow suit, trump if you can’t, and always try to beat the highest card so far.
Opponents may double (‘Kontra’) any part of the contract; the declarer may redouble.
scoring: Each part of the contract is won or lost separately; the declarer is paid by, or pays, both opponents. Typical values: Parti 1, 40-100 4, Ulti 4 (lose 8), Betli 5, Durchmars 6, 20-100 8. Hearts as trumps double the score.
Keep a running total; play a fixed number of deals.
variations: Open (‘Terített’) Betli and Durchmars are played with the declarer’s cards face up for higher scores. Unbid bonuses (e.g. silent ulti) also exist.

scorekeeper.hint: Zero-sum: the declarer gains or loses twice what each opponent does.

games.name: Toepen
equipment: A 32-card deck: 10, 9, 8, 7, A, K, Q, J of each suit (ranked in that order)
games.objective: Win the last of four tricks. Knock to raise the stakes and bluff others into folding. Lose ten lives and you’re out.
quickStart: Goal: win the 4th trick; don’t lose 10 lives.
Cards rank 10 (high), 9, 8, 7, A, K, Q, J. Follow suit if you can.
Knock to raise the stakes by a life — others must fold (lose lives now) or stay in.
setup: Deal four cards each. A player whose hand is all A/K/Q/J may swap it for a new hand — but others can challenge (the loser of the challenge loses a life).
gameplay: Left of the dealer leads. Follow suit if you can; otherwise play anything. The highest card of the suit led wins. There are no trumps.
Only the last (fourth) trick matters. Its winner deals next; everyone else still in loses a life.

Knocking: at any time a player may knock on the table, raising the stake by one life. Each other player must stay in or fold. Folding costs the lives at stake before the knock; staying in risks one more.
You can’t knock twice in a row; someone else must knock in between.
Fun rules: hold three 10s and you must whistle; four 10s and you must stand up.
scoring: Count lives lost. A player who loses 10 lives loses the game (traditionally buying a round). A player on 9 lost lives may not knock.
variations: Fast ‘drinking’ version: after a knock, everyone decides at the same time by throwing in their cards or not.

games.name: Zwicker
equipment: One standard 52-card deck plus three jokers, marked 15, 20 and 25 (55 cards)
Pen and paper or the score tracker
games.objective: Capture valuable cards from the table by matching, adding and building — especially the jokers. Clear the table for a ‘Zwick’.
quickStart: Goal: capture the most valuable cards (jokers, 10♦, Aces) with your partner.
Play a card to capture table cards of equal value or groups that add up to it — or start/modify a build.
Clearing the table is a Zwick, worth 1 point.
setup: Four players in partnerships, partners opposite.
Matching values: 2–10 face value; Ace 1 or 11; Jack 2 or 12; Queen 3 or 13; King 4 or 14; jokers 15, 20 and 25.
Deal four cards each and three face up on the table. Later deals: four more each, then five each.
gameplay: On your turn, play one card. You may capture any table cards it matches, or any groups adding up to its value — as many as you like.
Or build: place a card on a table card or pile, announcing the new total (by adding or subtracting), as long as you hold a card to capture it later. Your partner can build to your value too.
Or just leave your card on the table.
Capturing everything on the table is a Zwick. At the very end, the last team to capture takes any remaining table cards.
scoring: Large joker 7, middle joker 6, small joker 5, 10♦ 3, 10♠ 1, 2♠ 1, each Ace 1, most cards 3 — 30 per hand — plus 1 per Zwick.
Play a series of hands; the higher total wins.
variations: Older versions play without jokers; some play with six jokers.

games.name: Cuarenta
equipment: A 40-card deck: remove the 8s, 9s and 10s (keep them for scoring)
games.objective: Ecuador’s national card game. Capture cards by matching, adding and sequences; snap up your opponent’s last card for a ‘caída’. First to 40 points wins.
quickStart: Goal: first to 40 points.
Capture a table card by matching, or cards that add up to yours — then keep going up any sequence.
Matching the card just played is a caída (+2); clearing the table is a limpia (+2).
setup: Card order A, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, J, Q, K. For adding, Ace to 7 count face value; J, Q, K can only be matched.
Deal five cards each (four players play in partnerships). The rest is dealt five each when hands run out.
gameplay: On your turn, play one card. It captures a table card of the same rank, or (if a number card) a group of table cards adding up to it.
After a capture you may also take the next-higher card on the table, and the next, as long as the sequence is unbroken (e.g. play a 2 to take a 2, then 3, 4, 5).
Caída: capturing by matching the card the previous player just played scores 2. Limpia: clearing the table scores 2.
Ronda: being dealt three of a kind scores 4; four of a kind wins the game outright.
scoring: After all 40 cards: a side with 20 captured cards scores 6, plus 1 point per extra card (rounded up to even). If neither has 20, the side with more scores 2.
First to 40 wins. A side on 38 can’t score a limpia, so must finish with cards or a caída.
variations: Score is traditionally kept with the spare 8s, 9s and 10s laid face up.

games.name: Kop
equipment: 16 cards from a standard deck: the Aces, 10s, Queens and Jacks
games.objective: A fast Polish game with only 16 cards. The holders of the two black Queens are partners. Take at least 53 of the 104 card points.
quickStart: Goal: your team takes 53+ of 104 points.
Holders of the black Queens are secret partners (unless someone plays alone).
12 of the 16 cards are trumps; you must follow and beat the trick if you can.
setup: Deal four cards each.
Trumps (high to low): A♥, 10♥, Q♣, Q♠, Q♥, Q♦, J♣, J♠, J♥, J♦, A♦, 10♦. Only A♣, 10♣, A♠ and 10♠ are not trumps.
Card points: Ace 11, 10 10, Queen 3, Jack 2 (104 in all).
gameplay: Before play: anyone may double (‘Kontra’), and further doubles follow. A player may announce ‘Zolo’ to play alone against three, or ‘Zolo du’ to win all four tricks alone. A player with both black Queens may call ‘Wesele’ and partner the holder of the highest Jack they don’t hold.
